**Revised Version**  

The Polish course at the east branch library was structured around eight weeks, with sessions held on Thursday evenings. The instructor, a seasoned teacher, emphasized practicality: each week included a short explanation, guided exercise, and time for participants to experiment with changes.  

**Setup Challenges**  
A first issue arose when the projector displayed the library’s desktop instead of the laptop, and the cable was mislabeled. The instructor spent fifteen minutes searching for an adapter with the librarian, only to use the whiteboard for the first explanation and pass the laptop to the instructor when needed. The cable was the first problem, though the librarian initially assumed the issue was a simple technical glitch.  

**Learning Moments**  
The first exercise—printing a name and asking for a favorite food—felt too easy for some, while others struggled with brackets and quotation marks. When a small program added prices from a grocery list, the instructor wrote a line with incorrect indentation, stopping the session. A learner at the back noticed the issue, realizing the spaces were part of the instructions, not just formatting.  

**Week Three: Pairing Games**  
Pairs formed a number-guessing game, but the instructor planned a full outline. A few participants finished quickly, asking for a limit on guesses. One learner used a while loop, another tried if statements, and a third switched to a different approach. The instructor observed that the first version was confusing, while the second was clearer. A quiet learner also noted the change alone wasn’t enough.  

**Accessibility Adjustments**  
Accessibility tweaks came gradually: a student requested larger-print slides due to hard-to-read text, prompting a larger-print version and code-aloud explanations. Another learner mentioned the fluorescent lights made reading difficult, so the instructor moved their seat away from the brightest fixture. A third student, who preferred quiet work, asked for a shared workspace, which the instructor suggested but didn’t explain.  

**Week Four: Updates and Sharing**  
The library computers requested an update, and two machines restarted in the middle of the session. Learners saved their files to the desktop, but one person lost the version they’d changed. The instructor had not shown them how to save a second copy or where files would be stored. They spent time recovering examples from the shared folder, then added a reminder to save regularly. The instructor used a shared folder for the remaining weeks, but a machine couldn’t connect until the librarian signed in.  

**Exercises That Held Attention**  
The most engaging exercises were those involving grocery totals and quizzes with self-written questions. The temperature list was less popular, though it helped introduce lists and averages. A longer exercise with a book title file took longer than expected, but a student wrote a feedback card praising the clarity of the error explanation. A second student noted the pace was “a little fast,” while a third left their work blank, suggesting the timing was manageable.  

**Scheduling and Accessibility**  
The course faced uneven scheduling: a holiday closed the library for a week, moving the session to Wednesday. Four people couldn’t attend the new night, so the instructor sent notes and the exercise afterward. A learner also arrived late due to a bus connection, missing the opening explanation. The instructor began leaving the first example in the shared folder before class, which may have helped, but they didn’t ask directly about timing. The final session ended with a project, not a formal presentation, as two students preferred individual work.  

**Accessibility Tips**  
For a more inclusive experience, the instructor suggested a project should come earlier, allowing more time to work on it. A question about access needs could be asked beforehand, perhaps by the librarian. The project could also be scheduled earlier, with a clear plan for materials to move out.  

---

**Screening Details**  
The event was planned for Friday in early October, with doors opening at six and the film starting at seven. The room accommodated about sixty-five chairs, no stage, and a screen that rolled down to a set of old bookshelves. The film was a quiet, locally made documentary about a family-run ferry service, praised for its welcoming tone and ability to hold attention without being too long.  

**Film Selection**  
A shortlist of four films was chosen, with the DVD borrowed from the library. The film was watched at home with a notebook, and one title—beautiful outdoor scenes but nearly two and a half hours—was deemed too long for the evening. Another film relied on a joke that would have been difficult to explain, while a documentary about a family-run ferry offered enough detail for close attention without requiring specialized knowledge.  

**Rights and Logistics**  
The screening rights were unclear, with the library’s usual film license not specifying whether the event was a community screening. The distributor emailed the date, room capacity, and ticket price, and we waited days for a response. The first quote was higher than our refreshments budget, prompting a call to the distributor’s office. They offered a lower community rate, provided we didn’t advertise the event as free or make a recording. We shared these terms with the library coordinator before paying.  

**Captions and Accessibility**  
Captions mattered to regular visitors, so we checked the disc menu and the distributor’s listing. The DVD included English captions, but the first set was out of sync by a fraction of a second. We contacted the distributor again, learning the streaming version had a corrected caption file. We asked if we could receive the file separately, and they provided a replacement disc the following week.  

**Volunteers and Rotation**  
Eight volunteers helped on the night, with Mina and Rob setting out chairs, while Theo stayed near the entrance to greet people and answer questions. We also added two newer volunteers to handle tickets, as neither had used the cash box. The first two rows were open for extra space, and we marked a clear path to accessible seats. Just before doors opened, we counted chairs again and moved four away from the wall to accommodate wheelchair users.  

**Projector Test**  
The projector test occurred on Thursday afternoon, when the room was empty and quiet. Our borrowed laptop recognized it immediately, but the image was too wide, cutting off subtitles. We adjusted the display setting, changed the projector’s position, and replaced the strip of blue painter’s tape with a note on the remote. The opening scene with dark water was the most likely to reveal a focus or brightness issue.  

**Final Ticket Details**  
On Friday, the ticket table was ready by half past five. We charged a modest amount at the door and kept a handwritten list for those who reserved seats by email. A few guests paid with coins, so we brought a small envelope of change from the library office. We printed forty tickets, added blank slips for those who wanted more, and kept the room nearly full. Theo stopped taking payments long enough to help an older couple find two seats together. We did not sell the last few tickets, though the room looked busy from the back.  

**Rain and Weather**  
Rain began just as we carried the refreshments upstairs. We expected cool weather, but not a sudden downpour, and several people arrived with wet coats. The library’s entry mat was damp, so Mina fetched two extra towels and placed a notice near the stairs asking people to leave umbrellas by the door. Tea and apple juice were on the side table, along with biscuits from a bakery on the high street. We kept hot drinks away from the projector cables and moved the rubbish bin closer to the refreshments when wrappers began to collect.  

**Audience Interaction**  
The audience was quiet during the film, except for a brief laugh at a scene where the ferry’s bell rang while the owner was trying to give an interview. Afterward, several people stayed to discuss how the service had changed over the years. One guest ridden the ferry as a child and recognized the old ticket punch in a close-up. Another asked whether the director had filmed during winter crossings. I did not know, so I wrote down the question to send to the director rather than guessing. The discussion lasted about twenty minutes, and some guests continued it downstairs as they left.  

**Screening Invitation**  
For another screening, I would like to invite a local filmmaker to speak if the date and budget allow. We could also try a shorter film followed by a guided discussion, as people seemed comfortable sharing memories. I would reserve a few more seats near the front for those who need an unobstructed view, and I would test the captions on the exact equipment earlier in the week. The library has offered the room again in January, but we have not chosen a film or confirmed a date. For now, I have kept the distributor’s contact details, volunteer rota, and projector notes together in one folder.  

---
